system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-09-18 14:52:00 to 2174-09-21 10:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for persistent right shoulder pain following treatment for group B strep sepsis and polyarticular septic arthritis. Imaging revealed a lucency in the right humeral head suggestive of osteomyelitis. He underwent an incision and drainage procedure on 2174-07-31 under general anesthesia, tolerated it well, and had an uncomplicated postoperative course. Pain was managed with a transition from PCA to oral narcotics, and he was cleared for discharge to extended care on postoperative day one. He continues on clindamycin for infection, with instructions to perform pendulum exercises, keep the wound dry, and monitor for signs of complications. His cirrhosis and ascites were noted but stable during admission.
problems: Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Streptococcus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site, streptococcus, group B

A single 5mm stone that was causing partial obstruction was seen

A sphincterotomy was performed in the 12 o'clock position using

The stone and some sludge was extracted successfully using a

Brief Hospital Course:
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:  ___ presenting with right sided abdominal 
pain, CT evidence of CBD dilation, and LFT's consistent with 
bile obstruction most consistent with acute choledocholithiasis.
.

ERCP with papillotomy which would be diagnostic as well as 
therapeutic.  Patient put on empiric ciprofloxacin and flagy and 
made NPO except medications for surgery on hospital day Pain

Patient brought back to floor with much improved pain and no new

have his cell counts checked.
.

___.  Signs and symptoms of chronic liver disease 
include jaundice, mild confusion, and fatigue.  He was continued

Spiranolactone and tamoxifen held as patient was not volume

#.  Osteomyelitis:  Prior successful debridement on continued

You were admitted for abdominal pain which imaging demonstrated

put on IV antibiotics to prevent an infection and stabilized for

blood in stool or any other symptoms that are concerning as 
these will need immediate evaluation.

timing of surgery to remove your gall bladder.  ___ is the 
coordinator for surgery for Dr. ___.  ___.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAM:  PA and lateral chest ___.

INDICATION:  Severe abdominal pain.

CHEST, TWO VIEWS:  Comparison made to ___.  Heart size remains normal. 
Mediastinal and hilar contours are normal.  The lungs are clear.  Bilateral
calcified hilar granulomas are unchanged.  There is no sign of free
intraperitoneal air.

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary process.

HISTORY:  ___ man with acute onset of severe abdominal pain.  Please
evaluate for mesenteric ischemia.  Patient has known hepatic cirrhosis.

TECHNIQUE:  CTA abdomen with and without contrast, and 3D reconstructions.  No
oral contrast administrated.

COMPARISON:  Compared to abdominal ultrasound ___.

FINDINGS:

LUNG BASES:  No pleural effusion, pulmonary nodule or opacity is seen in the
lung bases.

CT ABDOMEN:  The liver is small and coarse, consistent with a clinical
diagnosis of cirrhosis.  There is no definite focal hepatic lesion.  The
gallbladder is distended.  There is extra- and intra-hepatic bile duct
dilatation, common bile duct measuring 8 mm, findings which could suggest
recent passing of a gallstone, or abnormality at the ampulla. There is no
definite radiopaque gallstone seen. There is fat stranding around the
duodenum, gallbladder, and pancreatic head. Findings should be correlated with
the laboratory tests, and for clinical evidence of questionable acute
cholecystitis, or bile duct obstruction.

The main portal vein is patent.  IVC is patent.

The spleen is enlarged measuring 16 cm in largest diameter, with focal
calcification likely from prior granulomatous disease.  There are multiple
collaterals between the portal and systemic circulation, likely consistent
with the patient's known diagnosis of cirrhosis.  There is fat stranding
around the pancreatic head.

There is no evidence of mesenteric ischemia.  The abdominal vessels are
patent.  There is no evidence of small-bowel obstruction. There is normal
appearance of the loops of small and large bowel, keeping in consideration
lack of oral contrast.  Kidneys enhance symmetrically.  There is no evidence
of hydronephrosis.  There is no evidence of large focal masses in the kidneys.
The adrenal glands are unremarkable.

There is no evidence of significant lymphadenopathy in the mesenterium or
retroperitoneum; however, there are some scattered mesenteric lymph nodes,
which do not meet the CT criteria for pathologic enlargement.  There is no
evidence of acute appendicitis.  There is some small amount of free fluid in
the abdomen. There is no evidence of free air in the abdomen.

CT PELVIS:  The visualized loops of small bowel, large bowel, sigmoid appear
within normal limits with some limitation due to lack of administration of
oral contrast.  There is a small amount of free fluid in the pelvis.  The
bladder appears unremarkable.  The prostate and seminal vesicles appear
normal.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  There are no suspicious lytic or sclerotic lesions in the
bones.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts dilatation.  Distended gallbladder.
Fat stranding around the gallbladder, duodenum and pancreatic head. Ascites.
Please correlate clinically for questionable bile duct obstruction,
cholecystitis, and with lab tests for pancreatatis. Findings were discussed
with Dr. ___ at 11:30 a.m, and posted on the ED dashboard.

2.  No evidence of small-bowel obstruction, or mesenteric ischemia.

3.  Portosystemic collaterals, and coarse and small liver with enlarged
spleen, findings consistent with known diagnosis of liver cirrhosis.

ERCP

COMPARISON:  None.

HISTORY:  Abdominal pain and abnormal LFTs and jaundice.

FINDINGS:  Seventeen fluoroscopic images were submitted for review without a
radiologist present.  These demonstrate mild proximal dilatation of the common
bile duct.  Per report, a common bile duct stone was extracted.  The
intrahepatic biliary tree was normal in appearance.

IMPRESSION:  Mild post-obstructive common bile duct dilatation. Extraction of
common bile duct stone per report.

Please see ERCP report for further details.

conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started yesterday morning—feels like I swallowed razorblades, right under my ribs on the right side. It hasn’t let up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea? Vomiting? Fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just nausea. No vomiting, no fever. But I’ve been feeling kind of yellow lately, and tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your liver enzymes are elevated, and the CT scan shows your bile duct is dilated. That suggests a blockage—likely a stone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stone? In my bile duct? Can that be fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re planning an ERCP tomorrow. It’s a procedure where we go in through your mouth with a scope to remove the stone. It’s both diagnostic and therapeutic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Through my mouth? That sounds intense. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very common and generally safe. You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything. The main goal is to relieve the blockage and prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds okay. What about my liver? I’ve had cirrhosis for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. The scan shows your liver is small and coarse, consistent with cirrhosis, and you have some fluid in the abdomen—ascites. But it’s stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my shoulder? I’m still on Bactrim for that old infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping you on Bactrim. Infectious disease wants you to continue it for your osteomyelitis. No signs of active infection now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want that coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure it doesn’t. For now, you’re on antibiotics—cipro and metronidazole—to prevent infection from the blockage. And you’ll stay NPO—nothing by mouth—after midnight for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Pain’s still pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll order IV Dilaudid to help. We’ll keep you comfortable until tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re scheduled for ERCP in a few hours. Any questions before we move forward?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—what happens if they can’t get the stone out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very likely they will. The imaging shows one small stone. If not, they might need to do it again or consider surgery later. But success rates are high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. The ERCP went great. They found a 5mm stone in your common bile duct and removed it with a balloon. The duct is now clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief! Is that why my pain’s already better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The blockage’s gone. They also did a sphincterotomy—cut the muscle a bit to help drainage and prevent future stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need my gallbladder out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, eventually. But not now. Your liver and overall condition make it safer to do it later, once you’re stable. Your PCP will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping cipro and metronidazole. Your white count dropped a bit, and with your history, we don’t want to suppress your bone marrow further. But you’ll keep taking Bactrim for your joint.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on lactulose to prevent confusion from liver disease. We held spironolactone and tamoxifen since you’re not swollen or having breast issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Ate clear liquids yesterday, now on a regular diet. Pain’s much better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, only mild discomfort now. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re stable, and we’ll send you home with pain meds and refills for your regular medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call your doctor or come back if you have fever, vomiting, severe pain, or jaundice. Also, avoid fatty foods for a few weeks—they can upset your digestion now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Bactrim—I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as prescribed. But see your PCP within a week to check your blood counts. That’s important with long-term antibiotics and cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’ve recovered well from the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Anything else I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your meds, avoid fatty foods, and follow up with your PCP. Call Dr. ___’s office to schedule gallbladder surgery when advised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and jaundice. Imaging revealed dilated bile ducts and lab findings consistent with biliary obstruction. He underwent an uncomplicated ERCP with sphincterotomy and successful removal of a 5mm common bile duct stone. His pain resolved post-procedure, and he tolerated advancement to a regular diet. His chronic hepatitis C and cirrhosis were stable, managed with lactulose; spironolactone and tamoxifen were held due to lack of volume overload. He remained on Bactrim for ongoing osteomyelitis prophylaxis, while ciprofloxacin and metronidazole were discontinued due to concern for bone marrow suppression. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with his PCP for blood work and surgical evaluation for cholecystectomy.

Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
